title: 1Password Security Incident
author: lxhrstn
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Update: We will be providing a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) with details in the coming weeks once our full investigation is complete.What happenedOn November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.What information was affectedThe attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:Names and email addressesAccount and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in timesPublic keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account) Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recoveryOther non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security. When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning. During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.What was not affectedYour vaults and the items in themThe keys that protect your vaults 1Password does not store your account password or secret keyAccount recovery keys1Password apps and browser extensionsWhat we’ve doneDisabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens. Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.What you can doBe cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts. 1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser. Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.Our commitment to youYou trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers. We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

comments.author: tptacek
comments.textRawHtml:
This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.

In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.

Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.

So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack.

I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

children.author: mikeocool
children.textRawHtml:
> You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.

You kinda have to wonder if this is necessary or true. I can’t say I’ve seen the rate of significant product improvements from SaaS providers increase this year (for 1Password in particular, I can’t think of one thing that had changed this year in the product).

However there has undoubtedly been an uptick in major outages and security incidents that have accompanied the increased rate of change.

children.author: edelans
children.textRawHtml:
> I can’t say I’ve seen the rate of significant product improvements from SaaS providers increase this year

This is my perception as well. And I have a lot of trouble reconciling this with the usage of AI I witness everyday (at personal level and professional level).

When you zoom in, we are shipping code faster than ever.

When you zoom out, appart from security breaches, I don't see such a significant impact in terms of features, UX, improvements...

Are we just using AI to build things that would never have been built in the first time?

children.author: mvkel
children.textRawHtml:
This is a reflection of the industry more than technical capability.

When you're first building something, you're in the innovator's dilemma; building something that someone needs but they're not asking for.

In a mature SaaS, the incentivized path is to build exactly what your customer is asking you for, because it minimizes churn. But the result is certainly less innovation.

Long term, software will look a lot more like it did in the 90s. Fully bespoke, but reliably maintained with AI. That is a transition we are witnessing now with the FDE/Field CTO position demand going up.

children.author: teiferer
children.textRawHtml: I don't think this is true. It only happens where you give in to the hype and let quality slip. You could do that before, having programmers rush stuff and skip reviews and testing etc. It might be harder to push back nowadays, but of course you can. "But then we are too slow" is not a convincing argument. You are slower than the alternative, which is to ship low quality rushed crap, but why be bothered by this? That flurry of incidents should just be a warning to everybody to just avoid that trap.

children.author: majormajor
children.textRawHtml:
> We are so far beyond that, the velocity demands are sky high from capital and the security/vuln risk.

Eh, ROI demands are sky high; the question `mikeocool` asked is whether or not code churn is actually contributing more to ROI today for established companies than a year or two ago.

I think the story on "max velocity vs revenue growth" is likely to play out very differently for 0->1, 1->10, and 10+customer type situations...

"We need to get these features out the door to win our first customers" is a clear ROI situation.

Shotgunning random crap at existing customers? Not so much. If the features don't have clear upsell opportunities to increase the value of those customers, then the customer retention question isn't simply "throw more updates at them and they'll stay."
